analysis.one_liner: Set federal patient-protection rules for managed-care plans and let patients sue for injury from denied care.
analysis.headline: The House passed a patient-rights bill 226-203 after rejecting a substitute backed by most Democrats, then the bill sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force employer health plans and insurers to follow rules for deciding claims, allow patients to appeal denials to an independent panel, guarantee direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care, and let patients sue in court for injury caused by a wrongful denial. The House passed an amended version on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate never voted on it and the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-based or insured health coverage, especially patients whose plans deny care — they would get faster decisions, outside review of denials, and the right to sue for injury.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must set time limits for decisions on claims and prior authorizations, with faster handling in emergencies [S3].
Patients denied coverage for medical reasons can appeal to an independent outside review panel whose decision is binding on the plan [S4].
Plans must cover emergency care without prior approval, allow direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care, and cover reasonable hospital stays after breast cancer surgery [S3].
Plans cannot gag doctors from advising patients about their condition or treatment, and cannot use doctor pay arrangements that reward denying care [S3].
The bill gives patients a federal right to sue for economic and noneconomic damages when a plan's careless denial of care injures or kills them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employer health plans and insurance companies, which would face new claim-handling rules, outside review costs, and court liability for wrongful denials; some of that cost could pass to premiums.

drawbacks.text: New coverage requirements and liability exposure could raise health insurance premiums for employers and workers [S3].
The bill expands medical savings accounts and gives full tax deductions to the self-employed, tax breaks that mainly help higher-income taxpayers [S2].
The right to sue applies only to non-medical decisions; medically reviewable decisions are handled by external review instead of court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are broad and address real complaints about denied care, but the bill also carries tax incentives — especially expanded medical savings accounts — whose benefits skew toward higher-income people, and the liability provision stops short of letting all denied patients sue in court.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in August 2001, the Senate put it on the calendar, and no Senate vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed H.R. 2563 on August 2, 2001, by a vote of 226 to 203 [S7].
The bill was placed on the Senate calendar in September 2001 and never came up for a vote [S6].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without the Senate acting, so the bill died [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plans avoided the new claim rules, outside-review obligations, and court liability, so they kept the existing system that favored them; self-employed taxpayers and small businesses also lost the tax deductions and credits the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Greg Ganske
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through House passage.

for.name: 220 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the House floor.

against.name: 202 of 208 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage after a Democratic substitute failed, objecting that the bill's liability and external review provisions were too weak compared with their preferred version.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 2563 to the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 220 of 223 Republicans voted yes, while only 5 of 210 Democrats did [S7].

industries.note: The bill subjects their claim and appeal practices to federal standards and lets patients recover damages for wrongful denials, raising their costs and litigation exposure.
Their plans would face the same compliance and liability rules, with possible premium increases passed to workers.

industries.industry: Health savings account providers and self-employed health insurance market
industries.note: The bill expands Archer medical savings accounts and lets the self-employed deduct health insurance fully, benefits that primarily help higher-income taxpayers rather than the broad patient population.
